exam: A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive man has a 6 mm induration. — Recognise this is positive (≥5 mm) and recommend isoniazid preventive therapy after ruling out active disease.
A 4‑year‑old child with prior BCG shows a 12 mm induration. — Explain this is likely a false‑positive; no treatment needed unless other risk factors exist.
A health‑care worker from a high‑TB burden area has a 16 mm induration. — State that any induration ≥15 mm is positive regardless of BCG, and discuss further evaluation for active TB.
A patient on steroids for lupus has a 4 mm induration. — Identify a possible false‑negative; advise repeat testing after tapering steroids or use IGRA.
You see a patient with a 10 mm induration but no known risk factors. — Explain that in low‑risk adults the cut‑off is 15 mm, so this is negative; no treatment required.
During a ward round you find a missing TST result sheet. — Emphasise the need to repeat the test because interpretation cannot be done without measurement.
A pregnant woman from a TB‑endemic region has a 8 mm induration. — Discuss that ≥10 mm is the cut‑off for pregnant women without other risk; this is negative.
A patient with active TB is started on treatment; the TST is still positive after 2 months. — State that TST does not become negative during therapy and should not be used to monitor response.
ai.title: Tuberculin Skin Test
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The tuberculin skin test (TST) detects delayed‑type hypersensitivity to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. Interpretation depends on induration size, risk factors, and local BCG vaccination prevalence.

b: Positive if induration meets risk‑adjusted cut‑off
Negative if no induration or <5 mm in low‑risk persons
sections.p: A small amount of purified protein derivative (PPD) is injected intradermally on the forearm. After 48–72 hours the induration is measured in millimetres.

t.b: What is the likelihood of latent TB infection? – Size ≥5 mm in HIV or recent contacts, ≥10 mm in immunocompetent with risk factors, ≥15 mm in anyone from high‑TB prevalence area.

b: Delayed‑type hypersensitivity (type IV) mediated by Th1 cells
Interpretation thresholds differ by HIV status, age, and exposure risk
sections.p: TST reflects a cell‑mediated immune response; a false‑negative can occur with immunosuppression, recent infection, or very young age. BCG vaccination may cause a false‑positive, especially with small indurations.

b: Identifies candidates for isoniazid preventive therapy
Helps decide on infection control measures in hospitals
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals TST remains a primary tool for screening health‑care workers, contacts of active TB, and HIV‑positive patients where IGRA is unavailable.

b: Remember BCG does not affect indurations ≥15 mm
sections.p: Examiners often test your ability to choose the correct induration cut‑off, recognise situations that invalidate the test, and outline next steps after a positive result.

b: Measuring the redness instead of the firm induration
Applying adult cut‑offs to children under 5 years
sections.p: Misreading the reaction, using the wrong measurement technique, or ignoring risk‑adjusted thresholds leads to misclassification.

whenToSeekHelp: Active TB symptoms (cough >2 weeks, weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis)
Severe hypersensitivity reaction at injection site
